idiom_name: dispatcher loop + performer pool + explicit dispatch policy
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: one component owns the dequeue step for the channel and, for every message, selects exactly one performer - from a fixed pool, by reusing a long-lived worker abstraction, or by creating a performer per message - and hands the message over. Keep the selection rule (round-robin, least-busy, affinity by key, specialist) behind one seam so performers stay policy-free, keep the queue bounded and define the behaviour at its bound, and keep failure semantics (retry, dead-letter, duplicate suppression) in the dispatcher instead of duplicating them in every performer. The classic structure is only warranted when performer selection is genuinely application logic; where the transport already assigns messages to consumers, or the runtime's own scheduler already dispatches, the coordinator collapses into configuration.
code_sketch:
channel = open_subscription(...)
pool = Worker Pool(n_performers)
policy = Dispatch Policy(...)
loop:
    msg = channel.dequeue()               # one owner of the dequeue step
    performer = policy.select(pool, msg)  # round-robin | least-busy | by key
    performer.hand_over(msg)              # exactly one performer processes it

on shutdown: channel.close(); pool.drain(timeout); report stragglers
pitfalls: Letting the dispatcher also process messages turns it into a performer and recreates the coupling the pattern removes.
An unbounded queue plus a fixed performer pool converts overload into memory growth instead of an honest rejection.
Selecting a performer per message but letting performers share mutable state reintroduces the races the coordination was meant to remove.

Wrong move: Put a local dispatcher in front of a broker consumer group that already assigns messages -> two coordinators obscure ownership and add a serial hop -> instead let the broker distribute and keep only genuinely local selection inside each consumer.

Wrong move: Treat an unbounded queue or unlimited prefetch as back-pressure -> overload becomes unbounded in-flight memory and latency -> instead bound capacity or prefetch and choose block, reject, drop, or dead-letter behavior.

Wrong move: Acknowledge or commit before the asynchronous performer finishes -> a crash after hand-off can lose work or break transaction assumptions -> instead define completion and acknowledgement timing plus retry/idempotency at the dispatcher boundary.
